query_text: A community-run archive and leaderboard app for creative writing prompts, living in the browser — where anyone can submit a prompt, vote on their favorites, and see a live ranking of the most-loved ones at the top. I want the archive side to let people browse prompts by category or tag, and the leaderboard to show who submitted the top-rated prompts this week. Something where the whole writing community feels like it's running the place together, and good prompts actually bubble up to the top over time.

A fan translation community app for indie manga and webcomics, for desktop browsers, where translators can claim a title to work on, upload translated pages chapter by chapter, and readers can browse finished translations by series or genre. I want a simple way for people to join translation teams, so multiple people can chip in on the same title, and readers can leave comments on chapters to cheer the translators on. The whole point is to give small indie works a chance to reach readers who speak other languages.

Make a color palette generator tool that lets you upload a photo or reference image and pulls out the main colors from it automatically, showing them as a neat row of color swatches with their hex codes right underneath — all in a web app you can use in your browser. You should be able to upload multiple images and compare the palettes side by side, and maybe click any swatch to copy the color code. Great for when you want to match colors from a photo you love for a craft project or design.

Create a podcast planner app that lets you map out each episode before you record — jot down the topic, guest name, talking points, and rough timing for each segment, all on one screen in the browser. Then on the other side of the same screen there's a show notes editor where you can write up the full notes for that episode, with spots for links and chapter markers. I want to keep every episode's plan and notes together in one place so nothing gets lost between planning and publishing.

Need a mood board builder app for desktop browsers where you can drag and drop images onto a big open canvas and move them around however you want, resize them, and layer them on top of each other. You should be able to pull in images by uploading files from your computer, and maybe also paste an image URL. I tinker with a lot of craft and color ideas and I want somewhere to just throw visual references together freely without everything snapping into a fixed grid.

Make a lyric writing app for desktop browsers where you have a big writing area to type out your song verses and choruses, and right alongside it there's a helper panel that suggests words that rhyme with whatever word you highlight, plus shows you the syllable count for each line as you write. I want to be able to flip between different sections of the song easily — verse one, chorus, bridge — so I can jump around while writing and keep everything organized without losing my place.

A YouTube thumbnail designer and side-by-side comparison app for desktop browsers where you can upload two versions of a thumbnail and see them both displayed at actual YouTube size, so you can judge which one pops more before uploading. The app should let you add a title text overlay on each thumbnail and pick from a few font styles to test how the text looks on the image. Really useful for figuring out which thumbnail catches the eye faster when you're staring at them both at the same time.

Need a brand kit generator app in the browser that walks independent creators through picking their brand colors, choosing a font pairing, and writing a short tagline, then spits out a tidy brand sheet at the end showing everything together — logo placeholder, color swatches with codes, font samples, and the tagline all on one page. Something you can share with someone as a clear reference for your whole look. Really handy for small creators who want everything to feel consistent without hiring a designer.

Create a newsletter template builder for desktop browsers aimed at indie writers and journalists, where you can pick a layout from a few clean options, then edit the text blocks, header, and footer right there on the page — no switching between tabs or separate editors. You should be able to see a preview of what the newsletter will actually look like as you type, and when you're done you can copy the finished template. Something that makes it easy to keep a consistent look across every issue without starting from scratch each time.

Create a writing samples site for a freelance copywriter — a web app that feels like a real portfolio with a personality, where each writing clip gets its own card showing the piece type, client industry, and a short excerpt, and visitors can filter by category to find what they're looking for. The whole thing should feel like it belongs to someone with a distinct voice and point of view, not like a generic resume page. There should be a short about section that sets the tone immediately, so the person's style comes through before anyone even reads a word of the work.

Need a portfolio website for an independent architect that feels serious and considered — the kind of site that earns trust before a word is read — where each project gets a full spread with photos, the project name, location, and a short description of what made it interesting, and any awards it won are shown cleanly alongside it. The site should work well in a desktop browser with a strong visual presence, letting the work carry the weight, so visitors don't have to dig around to find the good stuff.

Make a portfolio site for a freelance UX researcher — a web app that feels thoughtful and methodical, not flashy — where each project entry walks through the research process: the question being asked, the methods used, and what the findings actually led to, with sample deliverables shown inline like wireframes or summary reports. Visitors on desktop should feel like they're getting a clear window into how this person actually thinks and works, not just a list of company names they've worked with.

Create a personal site for an independent financial advisor that feels authoritative and clean — a web app that leads with credentials, certifications, and areas of expertise front and center, with a short bio that sounds like a real person wrote it, and a section that explains the kind of clients this advisor actually works with and what problems they help solve. The whole site should carry a sense of calm confidence, the kind of thing someone opens in their desktop browser and immediately feels like they're in capable hands.

Make a showreel site for a freelance videographer — a website that opens straight to a full-width video reel playing automatically, then below it a gallery of individual project entries each with a title, client name, and short description of what the video was for. The whole thing should feel cinematic and intentional, the kind of site that signals craft and care before anyone reads a word, and work beautifully on a desktop browser where the videos have room to breathe and show off the actual quality of the work.

Build a portfolio site for an independent brand strategist — a web app with a strong, confident feel, where each campaign entry shows the brand, the challenge, the strategy, and the results in a way that tells a clear story rather than just listing deliverables. The site should have a section that calls out notable numbers or outcomes from past work, because results are what actually matter, and it should look sharp on desktop so that when a potential client opens it in their browser, the whole thing reads like it was made by someone who really knows what they're doing.

Make a personal site for a freelance motion designer — a website that leads with a highlight reel of animation work right at the top, playing in a loop so visitors get a feel for the style immediately, then below that a list of past clients with the type of project done for each one. The whole thing should have a strong aesthetic identity that matches the kind of motion work being shown — not a bland template — and it should look great in a desktop browser where animations have the space to actually land the way they're meant to.

A thought leadership hub for independent business strategists — a website that feels like a proper editorial destination, not a blog, with a clean reading experience in the browser where big ideas get the space they deserve. The home screen of the site should surface the best and most recent pieces prominently, organized by theme so readers can follow the threads they care about, and each piece should feel authored and intentional with a byline and a clear point of view. The whole thing should carry a sense of intellectual seriousness that makes visitors want to stick around and read.

An archive site for expert interview transcripts and insights — a web app that feels like a genuine knowledge library in the browser, where each interview entry has the speaker's name, their area of expertise, the date, and the full transcript in a clean readable format alongside a set of key takeaways pulled out and highlighted for people who want the gist fast. Visitors should be able to browse by topic or speaker, and the whole thing should feel like a curated vault of real thinking, the kind of resource you keep bookmarked and come back to.

A story portfolio and pitching site for a freelance journalist — a website that carries a strong editorial identity right from the first glance, where each published piece is shown with the outlet it ran in, the story type, and a short description of why it mattered, so editors looking at it on a desktop browser can get a feel for the range and quality of the work immediately. There should be a separate section where the journalist can lay out what they're currently pitching or available to cover, so it works as a live calling card for potential editors, not just a static clip reel.

Need a subscription research report site for an independent analyst — a web app that feels serious and curated, where the homepage in the browser gives a clear sense of what the analyst covers and why their perspective is worth paying for, and subscribers can log in to read the full reports while free visitors see a teaser and a clear way to subscribe. Each report entry should show the topic, date, and a short summary that makes the argument for reading the whole thing, because the quality of the thinking should be evident before anyone commits.

Build a long-form essay site for a professional writer — a website with a very deliberate reading experience in the browser, where the essays are presented cleanly with generous text and no clutter, grouped into themes or ongoing series so returning readers can follow the threads that interest them most. There should be a short opinionated intro on the home screen that tells visitors exactly what kind of thinking they're going to find here, because the voice is the whole point, and each essay should carry a comments section where readers can respond to the ideas being put forward.

Need a template and resource library site for a consultant — a website that feels genuinely useful and well-organized in the browser, where visitors can browse templates and downloads by category, see a short description of what each resource is for and who it's meant to help, and grab the ones they need with a simple download. The whole thing should feel like it was built by someone who actually uses these tools and stands behind them, not a generic freebie dump, and returning visitors should be able to easily find new stuff that's been added since they last visited.

Build a writing samples and voice gallery site for an independent copywriter — a web app that has a real personality to it right from the first screen in the browser, where the work is grouped by tone and style so visitors can immediately see the range — playful, sharp, warm, authoritative — and click into examples to read the actual pieces. The site should feel like a demonstration of voice as much as a portfolio, so the writing speaks for itself, and there should be a short statement upfront that makes clear what makes this copywriter's style distinctly their own.

Build a photographer booking and pricing site — a website that feels warm and inviting in the browser, with a clear list of session packages showing what's included in each one, the price, and what kind of photography it's for, so potential clients can make up their minds without having to ask a bunch of questions first. There should be a simple calendar or booking form where someone can pick a date and type of session and send a request, and the whole thing should carry the photographer's personal style so it feels like meeting them before you even make contact.

Make a discovery call scheduling site for an independent coach — a web app in the browser that has a single clear focus: getting the right people to book a free first call, with absolutely no friction. The page should open with a short, direct statement about who the coach helps and what changes after working together, followed by a simple calendar showing available slots where someone can pick a time and confirm in under a minute. The whole thing should feel like it was made by someone with taste and conviction, not a generic booking page, so the person filling it out already feels good about the decision before they hit confirm.
